articles.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
articles.author: Jane Tavares, Senior Research Fellow and Lecturer of Gerontology, UMass Boston
paras: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?
The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.
While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.
Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements.

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.
Medicaid can help, but access is limited
Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.
However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services.
Who provides care in the meantime?
There’s a shortage of paid caregivers

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born.
The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.
Caregiving often has financial consequences
When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.
Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.
Families often have to shoulder responsibility

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have launched paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

articles.title: Preventable vision loss affects more than a billion people globally - and uneven access to care is the major culprit
articles.author: Joshua R. Ehrlich, Associate Professor and Population Health Scientist, University of Michigan
paras: Around the world, more than 1 billion people are living with vision loss in their daily lives. For many, this means they don’t have the glasses they need to see clearly. For others, conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration or diabetic eye disease have caused vision loss.
The burden of this problem is not shared equally – 55% of those experiencing vision loss are women and girls, 73% are ages 50 and older, and 90% live in low- and middle-income countries.

Age is the most important risk factor for vision loss. Since global populations are rapidly aging, the number of people experiencing vision loss is expected to increase to more than 1.7 billion by 2050.
So this public health threat is growing. Yet, it’s also almost entirely avoidable.

We are both population health researchers, and one of us is an opthamologist. We also lead the Michigan Sensory Health and Aging Research Collaborative at the University of Michigan, where we have spent years working to advance vision and eye health for underserved populations in the U.S. and globally. Recent developments give us hope that real progress is within reach.

Losing vision quite literally affects how people see the world, and it also increases their risk of other health issues, including falls, depression and even dementia. The risk of mortality is more than twice as high for adults living with vision loss.

The upside is that about 80% of vision loss can be reversed or prevented with timely detection and treatment. In fact, most cases can be fixed with eyeglasses or cataract surgery, two of the most cost-effective interventions in all of healthcare.

A recent report showed that eye care is not only important for health and well-being, but it is also a smart investment: Every dollar that low- and middle-income countries invest in eye health returns US$28 to their economies. This makes eye health easily one of the best deals in global health and development.
A development problem with a financial upside

Back in 1999, the World Health Organization launched an initiative called VISION 2020: The Right to Sight. The aim was to draw attention and resources to vision and eye health problems, including those that would affect an aging global population.

More recently, in 2021, 193 United Nations member countries unanimously ratified a resolution calling on governments and international financial institutions to improve access to eye care and to provide the resources to make this possible.

In addition, this resolution acknowledged the central role of vision and eye health in achieving the U.N. sustainable development goals, a set of 17 ambitious aims, including universal access to food, clean water, education and work. Reframing vision and eye health as a development issue with a massive financial upside put the problem in front of people from a variety of sectors, such as education, labor and economics, and encouraged them to imagine how they could be a part of the solution.

In the five years since that resolution passed, the eye health sector has evolved some innovative strategies. For example, the new Vision Catalyst Fund brings together large-scale donors, nongovernmental organizations and local medical providers to test new approaches to paying for eye care and getting it to those most in need.

Another organization that has emerged to tackle avoidable vision loss is Peek Vision, a U.K.-based charity that began as a simple smartphone app. This app can be used by anyone with access to a smartphone to screen vision. So far, it has been used to screen more than 18 million people for vision loss and has connected more than 1.5 million to eye care. The organization is hoping to screen a million people per week by 2029.

In November 2026, the government of Antigua and Barbuda hosted the first-ever Global Summit for Eye Health, in collaboration with the governments of Nigeria, Guyana, Ireland and Bangladesh and the WHO. Policymakers, nongovernmental organizations, heads of state and global organizations such as the U.N., WHO and World Bank attended, with an eye toward a singular goal – ending avoidable sight loss worldwide.

The summit’s goal was to bring together key players from across the eye health sector. Governments and organizations are being asked to make forward-looking commitments toward accelerating progress. For example, 48 governments committed to embedding eye health in their national health systems, while health ministries, NGOs and eye hospitals have committed to providing cataract surgery and eyeglasses to tens of millions of people over the next few years.

The evidence to drive this investment is already there: Trials have shown that vision care for kids boosts educational outcomes. In middle-aged and older adults, research shows that an inexpensive pair of reading glasses boosts productivity and economic earnings in the agricultural, garment and artisan industries.
Affording eye care in the US

While low- and middle-income countries contend with the overwhelming majority of vision loss, the problem is also significant in the U.S., where an estimated 32.2 million people contend with vision loss.

Older adults are by far the most affected group. While they benefit from Medicare coverage for medical issues such as cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration, major gaps remain, including unequal access to advanced eye care and inconsistent coverage of eyeglasses by Medicare.

Under traditional Medicare, eyeglasses are covered only once in a beneficiary’s lifetime, following cataract surgery. Otherwise, glasses can be a large – and recurring – out-of-pocket expense. With a pair of glasses costing an average of US$200-$370 in the U.S., compared with roughly $35 in China or India, clear eyesight may be financially out of reach for many older Americans. Low-cost online retailers have helped to disrupt this market, but accessing glasses through those websites still requires internet access and a credit or debit card.

Older adults dealing with common issues such as cataracts or refractive error, which causes blurry vision, are at higher risk for all sorts of costly downstream health issues, including falls and dementia. Each year in the U.S., 2.3 million older adults wind up in the ER for a fall, and nearly 1 million are admitted to the hospital, costing the healthcare system about $20 billion. When it comes to dementia, the costs are even greater, at around $750 billion dollars per year.

Financing more comprehensive eye care for older Americans is actually in everyone’s best interest. In fact, every dollar that public programs such as Medicare invest in treating refractive error and cataracts in older Americans is likely to return $9 to the U.S. economy. Annually, this equates to around $23 billion. This return on investment comes in the form of increased economic productivity, medical cost savings, fewer falls and fewer people with dementia.

Being able to see clearly is essential to overall health and well-being. The data is clear, that regardless of a country’s level of wealth, it makes sense to put resources toward vision and eye health.
Joshua R. Ehrlich receives funding from The US National Institutes of Health and has received an honorarium from AARP.

articles.title: Paid sick leave laws are no guarantee for Philly’s immigrant restaurant workers
articles.author: Ewa Protasiuk, Assistant Professor of Sociology, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
paras: What do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day.

There is no federal right to paid sick leave. However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide, requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees.
In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck.
For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy.

I study restaurant work, an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born. Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala.

I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez.

Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015. During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act, a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees.

A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees.
What I found, though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers.

Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “reasonable documentation” – but only after an absence of more than two days.
Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance.

If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them.

Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.”

What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said.
Different policies for back-of-house workers

In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America.

The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid.

In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white.
I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers.

“The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.”
In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born.

Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about.

Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves.

“The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’”
Healthy workers, healthy public

My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California.

Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. Paid sick leave makes for healthier workers, and healthier workers make for a healthier public.

articles.title: Alcohol addiction and eating disorders often go hand in hand – here’s why
articles.author: Anna Preece, PhD Candidate, Disordered Eating and Alcohol, Bournemouth University
paras: When some people drink, they purposely skip meals in order to amplify the effects of the alcohol or to save calories for their drinks. The practice, sometimes referred to as “drunkorexia”, highlights the crossover that can exist between risky drinking behaviour and disordered eating.

Although this practice has been documented in students and “wine-mom culture”, very little research has actually investigated how common it is in people who are in alcohol treatment services. This is what my research sought to do.

My colleagues and I recently conducted a review which found that eating problems are common among people being treated for alcohol addiction. We also found that the two conditions often share the same underlying drivers.
We reviewed data from 44 studies published between 1988 and 2026. Most of the studies were conducted with women living in high-income countries, including the US, Canada and the UK.

All the studies involved people getting support for their drinking. Some studies also included people getting support for their eating behaviour, while others only asked participants to fill in questionnaires about their eating habits.

Most studies were observational. This meant that rather than testing a treatment, people within these services were observed and asked about their experiences. This means our findings only show a link – we cannot prove cause and effect.
We found that people who are receiving treatment for alcohol use problems have around twice the likelihood of experiencing an eating disorder compared with the general population.

For instance, one of the studies we included in our review found that over two-thirds of women who were receiving treatment for alcohol addiction identified as binge eaters, while between 6% and 39% had bulimia nervosa.

Using food to cope with difficult emotions, manage mood or as a substitute for alcohol was common among both men and women undergoing treatment. Traits such as impulsivity, low self-esteem and negative self-image were common among study participants as well.

Several of the papers also showed that difficulties with mental health, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were linked with increased risk of struggling with both an eating disorder and alcohol addiction.

Our study also showed that people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction who are struggling with eating problems may be at increased risk of leaving treatment early, against medical advice. This can make recovery harder, increase the severity of challenging eating behaviour and the risk of medical complications.
Overall, our review highlights the distinct link between both alcohol addiction and disordered eating, and the common underlying traits both may share.

Our findings also suggest that asking people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction about their eating behaviour could support treatment and highlight any challenges a person may be experiencing sooner.
Both eating disorders and alcohol addiction can affect how the body absorbs nutrients, which may lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Weight gain may also be a problem in alcohol recovery, especially if a person uses sugar or food in order to cope. People who struggle with both of these conditions may also be at greater risk of depression or anxiety.
Using food and drink to cope with stressors, low mood or feeling bad about yourself is common – but many people may not be aware of when this behaviour becomes unhealthy or out of control.

For those undergoing treatment for alcohol use disorder, it may be beneficial to share any questions or concerns you may have surrounding food or eating with your therapist or nurse – including any challenging emotions you may have about food or meals.
Understanding the way both alcohol use disorder and disordered eating are connected means we may be able to better help those undergoing treatment for either condition.

articles.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer’s?
articles.author: Rahul Sidhu, PhD Candidate, Neuroscience, University of Sheffield
paras: A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.
These drugs affect blood flow and other processes that may play a role in brain health. An experimental drug called AR1001 has produced encouraging results in a large international clinical trial.
In one group of people with early Alzheimer’s, the drug was reported to slow the worsening of symptoms by 31% over a year, compared with a placebo.

AriBio, a South Korean biotechnology company, announced the results at the 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston, US. A full scientific paper, reviewed by other researchers, has not yet been published.
The phase three trial – the final phase of testing in humans – involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s in 13 countries. Participants took either 30mg of AR1001 or a placebo every day for a year.

Researchers measured changes in memory, thinking and everyday activities. They looked at two groups: everyone who took part in the trial and a smaller group of 604 people who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines to ease their symptoms, such as donepezil or memantine.
Only this smaller group saw a 31% reduction in worsening symptoms. Across the whole trial, AR1001 did not produce reliable benefits.
How could erectile dysfunction drugs affect the brain?

Erectile dysfunction drugs work by blocking an enzyme that normally breaks down a chemical messenger – called cGMP – in the body. This allows cGMP to build up, helping the muscles around blood vessels relax. The vessels widen, allowing more blood to flow through them. This is how the drugs help treat erectile dysfunction.

The same chemical messenger also helps brain cells communicate with each other. Researchers think that increasing its levels could help brain cells survive and maintain the connections they need to share information.

These connections are essential for learning and memory. Alzheimer’s gradually damages them, making it harder to remember things and think clearly. Researchers hope that AR1001 might help protect some of these connections and slow the damage caused by the disease.
However, this is still a theory. The clinical trial does not show that these biological changes explain the reported benefits in people.

Some laboratory and animal studies support the idea. In a 2022 study, mice with features of Alzheimer’s disease performed better in memory tests after receiving AR1001. The treatment also reduced levels of amyloid-beta and abnormal tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s.

Other experimental research in mice has found that AR1001 can increase levels of cGMP and a protein that helps brain cells survive. However, results in animals do not always translate into benefits for humans.

Interest in this family of drugs has also grown following research in people. A 2024 study followed more than 269,000 men with erectile dysfunction. It found that men prescribed these drugs were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s than men who were not prescribed them.
But this was an observational study, which means it cannot show that the drugs themselves reduced the risk of Alzheimer’s. The two groups may have differed in other ways that influenced the results.
A complicated relationship

The relationship between erectile dysfunction and Alzheimer’s is complicated. Erectile dysfunction can be associated with conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, which can damage blood vessels. These same conditions are also linked to poorer brain health and a higher risk of dementia.

This means that some of the apparent link between erectile dysfunction, its treatments and dementia could be down to shared risk factors affecting blood vessels, rather than a direct effect of the drugs.
Erectile dysfunction drugs are not an established treatment for Alzheimer’s, and nothing in these results suggests people should take them to protect their memory.
The latest trial does, however, keep alive an interesting possibility: that drugs that improve blood flow and help brain cells communicate might also slow the damage caused by Alzheimer’s.

Whether this is the case will depend on the full trial results and further research in people, including studies looking at why the apparent benefit was seen only among those not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.

articles.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
articles.author: Hannah Campbell, Lecturer in Applied Human Physiology | Researcher Female Health in Sports, Exercise & Physical Activity | Registered Clinical Exercise Physiologist, University of Leeds
paras: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

As you lift the bag, your brain sends signals that tell your muscles when to tighten and how hard to pull. At the same time, signals from your body help your brain tell where your limbs are and whether you’re starting to lose your balance. If the bag is heavier than you expected, you can adjust your grip and shift your weight as you lift.

A recent study involved 162 adults aged 65 and over who showed signs of mild cognitive impairment. This means having more difficulty with memory or thinking than is usual at that age while still being able to manage most everyday tasks.

The researchers compared gentle exercise with a 24-week programme of resistance training, in which muscles work against a weight or against the body’s own weight. The strength exercises gradually became harder. In the second half of the programme, participants began doing some of them on surfaces such as foam pads, which made it harder to keep their balance.

By the end of the programme, the strength-training group scored slightly higher than the gentle-exercise group on two tasks: repeating a string of numbers immediately after hearing it and naming as many words as possible beginning with the letter A in one minute. The groups scored similarly when asked to remember details from a story, both immediately and half an hour later. It’s unclear whether the small differences on the two tests would make a difference in daily life. Whether the programme affects the chances of developing dementia, where changes in memory or thinking interfere with daily life, remains an open question.

When someone first starts strength training, they can get stronger before their muscles grow noticeably. One reason is that the brain and nerves get better at activating the muscles needed for the movement. Think of it as developing a “muscle map”. With practice, it becomes easier to sense where your body is and adjust how much effort you need.

An exercise that challenges your balance may also demand more attention. Whether that extra effort benefits other thinking skills is less clear. In the 24-week study, the researchers compared the whole training programme with gentler exercise, so they couldn’t tell how much the balance challenge itself contributed to the results.

Much of the research on exercise and thinking skills in older age looks at memory or at skills such as planning and switching between tasks. Those tests can tell us how someone performs on a particular task. Other measures are needed to see whether exercise helps someone move more confidently or manage everyday activities on their own.

Practising one task can make a similar task easier. For example, doing squats can help you stand up from a chair because both movements use many of the same muscles. The same principle applies to thinking skills. Strength training might give you practice at remembering the order of your exercises, while a programme designed to improve memory gives you more direct practice at learning new information and recalling it later.
How strength training might affect the brain

Strength training may also affect the brain through changes elsewhere in the body. It can lower blood pressure and help the body respond better to insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. Both high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes are linked to a higher risk of dementia.

Strength training may also reduce some signs of long-lasting inflammation, which can occur when the body’s immune defences stay active over time. Researchers are still investigating what that might mean for the brain.

Other studies have looked at whether strength training changes the levels of proteins that help brain cells work and form connections. Some have found higher levels of these proteins in the blood after training, but results in people have varied. When muscles tighten during exercise, they also release substances called myokines, which can send signals to other parts of the body. Researchers are exploring whether some of those signals affect the brain.

Strength training can help some older adults who have difficulty getting around to move more easily. That might make it easier to walk to the shops or get to a regular social activity. Over time, those outings could provide more opportunities to stay active and see other people. Being physically inactive and being socially isolated are both linked to a higher risk of dementia. What someone can do with their improved strength also depends on practical things, such as how easy it is to get somewhere and how confident they feel going out.

More women than men live with dementia worldwide, yet women are less likely to do regular strength exercises. A review drawing on studies involving more than 2.6 million adults estimated that fewer than one in four did muscle-strengthening exercises at least twice a week. In interviews with women who trained regularly, some described feeling unsure of their abilities or feeling that strength training was seen as something for men.

Having the chance to build strength and confidence earlier in life can help people stay independent as they get older. The benefits can show up in ordinary ways, whether it’s carrying the shopping home or getting out of a chair without help.

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs could free up an area of farmland larger than Italy – new study
articles.author: Roslyn Henry, Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen
paras: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land – an area slightly larger than Italy – for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift towards healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease”, blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government commissioned national food strategy, finalised in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.
Changing the food system alongside medicine

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use and the environment.

Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

articles.title: A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP-1 medication
articles.author: Reed Berger-Fleishman, Associate Clinical Professor of Medicine and Surgery, University of Illinois Chicago
paras: Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends.

But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts.

For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.

As a physician specializing in obesity medicine, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage.

However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love.

Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb.

GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer. Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol.

In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging.

One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing fullness signals. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate.

These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving.
GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors.

Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience.
Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment.

Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions:
Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication.
Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal.
Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion.
Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms.
The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms.
Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment.

Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don’t assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time.

If you’re flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to carry them on.

Arrange prescription refills in advance. If you anticipate needing a refill while traveling, contact your pharmacy and prescribing clinician ahead of time. Prescribing and dispensing regulations can complicate obtaining medications in another state, so don’t wait until you run out.

Stick to your regular dosing schedule. Don’t take an extra dose or double up on medication to accommodate a holiday meal or try to suppress your appetite further. Taking more medication than prescribed can increase the risk of significant side effects and potentially cause an overdose. If travel disrupts your dosing schedule or you miss a dose, follow the instructions for your specific medication, or contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist.
When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own.
Don’t sweat it with the occasional treat
Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made.

You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective.

At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward.

articles.title: What is ‘intergenerational trauma’? A social worker explains how one generation’s experiences can affect descendants
articles.author: Jaclyn Kirsch, Professor of Social Work, University of Texas at Arlington
paras: Throughout history, millions of people have experienced widespread violence, persecution and loss. During the Holocaust, 6 million Jewish people were murdered. Beginning in 1619 and through the mid-1800s, 12.5 million African people were forced onto ships during the trans-Atlantic slave trade. These are just two examples of many that have affected communities in ways that last long after the initial experiences.

Such traumas can have lasting consequences for a person’s physical and mental health. Yet, these effects may extend beyond those directly affected. Some can change the psychological, emotional and social well-being of a person’s children and grandchildren.
This phenomenon, known as “intergenerational trauma,” describes how the effects of trauma can extend across generations. This can occur even when descendants have not experienced the original events.

Intergenerational trauma can come from individual experiences, such as childhood abuse or family violence. But researchers have primarily studied it in relation to collective experiences. These can include genocide, enslavement, colonization, war or forced displacement – when unrest or famine force people to leave their homes.

I am a professor of social work. My research with immigrants and refugees looks at how collective and historical traumas shape individual and community well-being across generations. My work also explores how culture helps people cope with hardship, heal and recover together as groups.
How trauma crosses generations

Intergenerational trauma gained wider attention in the 1990s. Studies of Holocaust survivors and their children helped bring the issue to light. Researchers in the United States, Europe and Israel studied families affected by persecution, displacement and profound loss. They explored how these events shaped the mental health of descendants who had never lived through them.

Over time, scholars have found multiple relational paths through which the consequences of trauma can extend across generations. For example, fear can shape parenting, and a parent’s silence can make their distress hard to understand. Trauma can also weaken community ties.

Biological changes may also occur through what’s called epigenetics. These changes can affect how cells use genes while leaving the DNA code intact. This may also help explain how the effects of trauma reach later generations.

A study of three generations of Syrian refugee families, for instance, found a link between exposure to wartime violence and chemical marks on DNA. Scientists still don’t know whether parents can pass these marks to their children or if they affect how their children respond to stress.
Lasting effects of collective and historical trauma
Recognizing intergenerational trauma helps trace how experiences affect entire communities, not just individuals.

Closely related is the concept of “historical trauma” or “collective trauma.” These describe the cumulative effects of collective experiences, not just one-time events, over time. Examples are colonization, genocide and ongoing discrimination and mistreatment across generations.

For example, researchers have studied how colonization and family separation continue to affect the mental, social and physical health of generations of Indigenous peoples. They have looked at the lasting effects of government policies that forced Indigenous people to adopt the dominant culture. These policies barred people from speaking their own languages and practicing their traditions.

In Canada, for instance, First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were forcibly sent to residential schools between 1831 and 1997. Studies have linked their attendance to psychological distress among descendants.

Likewise, in the U.S. in the 19th and 20th centuries, the federal government operated or supported Native American boarding schools. Research shows a link between fathers’ attendance and chronic health problems in their adult children.

In Australia, researchers have found higher rates of mental health problems among descendants of the “Stolen Generations.” These were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families from the mid-1800s into the 1970s.

Among Black Americans, scholars have shown how the historical legacies of enslavement and racial violence intersect with current experiences of racism. These collective experiences may shape family narratives, cultural identity and psychological well-being across generations.

Many immigrant and refugee communities also experience historical trauma. A review of studies on collective trauma among forced migrants displaced by war, persecution or political violence shows they often navigate the effects of loss and separation long after they move to a new country.

Research has identified parental distress, cultural identity and changing family roles as ways these experiences affect descendants. Similarly, colleagues and I examined previous research that also highlights how these effects can shape the lives of subsequent generations of migrant families.

Across these populations, intergenerational trauma involves more than the passing on of psychological distress within families. When subsequent generations experience discrimination or continued threats to their cultural identity, the consequences of past trauma can intersect with new hardships.
From intergenerational trauma to intergenerational resilience
Just as the consequences of trauma can extend beyond the generation that experienced it, so can resilience.

In my work with immigrants and refugees, I have found that intergenerational trauma is neither inevitable nor uniform across communities. Psychological outcomes vary among descendants of trauma survivors. For instance, in one study of adult children of Holocaust survivors, about 1 in 3 had experienced post-traumatic stress disorder if both parents had it. Fewer than 1 in 10 had experienced PTSD if neither parent had it.
Families and communities pass down cultural traditions, stories of survival, collective healing and shared identities too. These can help future generations navigate adversity.

An intergenerational trauma perspective recognizes that healing involves families and communities. It may mean addressing pain within groups and offering mental health care that respects culture. These can be community-based approaches that create opportunities for shared understanding, connection and healing.

Individuals and communities do not need to be defined by the suffering of their ancestors. Rather, the concept of intergenerational traumas helps recognize how past experiences can continue to shape the present. It also acknowledges that these influences do not determine the future.
The experiences of previous generations can leave lasting wounds. But they can also provide foundations for strength, connection and healing.

articles.title: Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes therapies show great promise – but treatment is only effective if people can access it
articles.author: Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, Associate Professor of Health Promotion and Policy, UMass Amherst
paras: In 2026, over 830 million people worldwide are estimated to live with diabetes – more than ever before.

Most live in low- and middle-income countries, and over 90% live with Type 2 diabetes, a condition where the body cannot use insulin properly. The second most common form of diabetes is Type 1, caused by the immune system attacking insulin-producing cells.

A 2023 analysis used existing data to model the future burden of diabetes. It estimates that by 2050, more than 1.3 billion people will have diabetes. In North Africa and the Middle East, nearly 17% of people may be affected. In Latin America and the Caribbean, that number could be 11%. Diabetes increases risks of dying early as well as developing a range of complications, including eye, kidney and heart disease. It also affects mental health and well-being.

Despite these climbing numbers, there are plenty of reasons to be hopeful about the future of diabetes. I like to regularly remind myself of them, as a healthcare researcher who has lived with Type 1 diabetes for over 30 years.

New treatments are on the horizon, and high-profile people with diabetes are speaking about the condition, raising awareness of the need for better treatments and access to care. In September, Alexander Zerev won the U.S. Open tennis championship; in October, Garret Mitchell won the baseball World Series; and in November, James Talarico was elected to the U.S. Senate. Talarico has used his experience to advocate for lower insulin costs, as has New Hampshire representative-elect Stefany Shaneen, whose daughter lives with Type 1.
The search for a cure for Type 1 diabetes

There is no one single cause of either type of diabetes. Genetics, age, race, ethnicity, weight, smoking, diet and physical activity can all contribute to the development of Type 2. Type 1 is thought to be caused by genetics and the environment. Without being able to pinpoint one specific cause, cures have largely proved elusive.
When I was diagnosed in the early 1990s, I was told that a cure for Type 1 would be on its way in the next few years. Some 30 years later, a cure that works for most people has yet to arrive.
But promising results are coming out for treatments in which insulin-producing cells are either grown in a lab or taken from people who have died and then transplanted into people with Type 1.

In clinical trials, the majority of people receiving transplanted insulin-producing cells either no longer needed insulin or could take significantly lower doses. Reducing the amount of insulin they needed reduced their chance of developing severely low blood sugar levels, which can be fatal.

The challenge, though, is the risk the body will recognize the new cells as foreign and launch an immune response against them. For people with Type 1, the risk is even greater because their body has already attacked its own insulin-producing cells, meaning their immune systems already see insulin-producing cells as foreign. Medications can help, but for most people, the risks of a lifetime on immunosuppressants outweigh the benefits of living without Type 1 diabetes.

Other new and exciting developments are afoot, though. These include changing the cells before they are implanted so the immune system won’t attack them in the first place, as well as using targeted medications that would stop the immune system from attacking insulin-producing cells without making someone immunocompromised – in other words, leaving the rest of the immune system intact.
Treatments that delay progression of type 1 diabetes – rather than just treating its symptoms – are already available.

In the past few years, research has shown that the drug teplizumab can delay the progression of Type 1 diabetes by slowing down the destruction of insulin-producing cells in people whose immune systems have started to attack them. This can delay the need to start insulin for up to three years. Those three years allow people and their families time to plan. And they give children time to mature and live life without insulin injections, blood sugar checks and all the disruption that diabetes can bring.

Type 1 diabetes has no known single cause, but you’re more likely to get it if a close family member has it. In the U.S., people who don’t yet have symptoms can be screened for early Type 1 if a family member lives with the disease.

A blood test can identify the body’s attack on insulin-producing cells far before any symptoms show up, and before blood sugars start rising. If you’re at risk of Type 1 because a family member lives with it, you can either take a sample of your blood at home and send it to a lab, or have the sample drawn at a doctor’s office. It is then sent away for special testing to see if the blood contains markers that show the immune system is targeting insulin-producing cells. This allows people to get early treatment with drugs that can slow the progression of Type 1 diabetes.

My kids received a blood test at their doctor’s office through a program called TrialNet, a long-running research partnership that operates across North America, Europe and Australia. We received the results within weeks and found that neither of them had early signs of Type 1 diabetes at the time. We will retest every few years – though they don’t have signs now, their immune systems could start targeting their insulin-producing cells in the future.
Because 90% people diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes don’t have a family member who lives with it, European experts are calling to roll out screening for everyone, not just those at heightened risk.
More effective treatment programs for Type 2 diabetes

Science also offers reasons to be hopeful when it comes to Type 2 diabetes. A clinical trial published in October 2026, involving nearly 100 people with early-onset Type 2, found that over half of participants saw their diabetes go into remission six months after starting a low-calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Similarly, a 2025 study showed that an AI-driven mobile application providing personalized lifestyle advice for diet, physical activity and sleep led to sustained remission in over half of participants for up to three years.

New studies are also showing that GLP-1 medications not only lower blood sugar, but they also reduce deaths, hospitalizations and amputations in high-risk populations with Type 2 diabetes. Other recent studies have shown that GLP-1s can prevent the onset of Type 2 in people with elevated blood sugar levels.
Unequal access to treatment
However, these causes for hope only lead to meaningful change when healthcare is available.

Because of lack of access to testing, researchers estimate that more than 250 million people worldwide are unaware that they live with Type 2 diabetes. This means that they can’t make efforts to reverse or treat it.
Only about 1 in 2 people across the globe with Type 2 diabetes have access to the insulin they need. GLP-1 access is concentrated in high-income countries, and costs can be prohibitive.

Similarly, screening and early treatment for Type 1 diabetes are rarely available across low- and middle-income countries. There is no doubt that if and when a cure comes, many will not be able to access it.
My team’s research found that the COVID-19 pandemic made it even more difficult for people to access diabetes care.

A nonprofit group I work with called T1International regularly surveys people living with diabetes about their ability to access their essential supplies. In its latest survey, more than a third of the over 1,000 participants had rationed their diabetes supplies in the past year because of cost.
But here again, research offers hope.
Scientists are looking for ways to make insulin easier to manufacture and distribute. Growing attention on improving access to insulin and diabetes care could provide a powerful catalyst for change.
In 1923, Frederick Banting, the Canadian scientist who co-discovered insulin, famously sold its patent for one Canadian dollar, saying “Insulin is not for me, it is for the world.”
Much still needs to be done to achieve that vision – not only for insulin, but for the new scientific discoveries in the pipeline.

Jamie Hartmann-Boyce has received diabetes-related research funding from the World Health Organization, the British Heart Foundation, and the University of Oxford. She is a research fellow (unpaid) with T1International.

articles.title: Paramedics need time and support to recover between emergency calls
articles.author: Rebekah Haimes, Lecturer in Paramedic Science, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: When a paramedic arrives at your door, they may have come straight from someone else’s emergency. “I don’t know how you do your job,” people often tell me. I think about how little time there can be to take in what’s happened on one call before the next one comes in.

I’m a paramedic and an academic specialising in paramedic science. Ambulance staff deal with death and serious injury, and they can encounter violence on the job. There are pressures between calls, too. A review of research on ambulance work describes how long shifts, unpredictable work and limited time to recover can add to the strain.

In a separate UK study carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic, ambulance staff reported worsening shortages and raised concerns about having too little time to do the job. In ambulance work, there’s an expectation that we’ll be resilient and raise a hand if we’re struggling. I find that second part difficult, and I doubt I’m the only one.

Researchers describe resilience as a process of adapting in the face of serious adversity. When I hear that we’re expected to be resilient, I think of something springing back into shape. I’m uneasy about applying that image to people. I can be ready to help the next patient and find, at the end of my shift, that I’m still thinking about the previous call. If getting on with the job is taken as a sign that we’ve recovered, it falls to us to say when the strain is getting too much.

I prefer to think about fortitude – the strength and courage it takes to face the demands of the work. That can include telling someone when a call has stayed with you. What interests me is where that strength comes from. Having a colleague you trust and time to talk can make it easier to say how you’re doing before the strain builds any further.
When it’s hard to give patients the care they need

Paramedics describe caring well for patients as one of the most rewarding parts of the job. That same commitment could make some calls especially painful. When staff felt unable to give a patient the care they believed was needed, they described a strain known as moral distress. It’s what you can feel when something prevents you from doing what you believe is right.

A separate study looked at how paramedics decide when to stop trying to revive a patient whose heart has stopped. Some described following guidelines that required them to keep going even when they believed further attempts would do no good. The guidelines are there to protect patients. Following them can still be difficult when a paramedic’s judgement about the person in front of them pulls in a different direction.
A conversation after a difficult call can help a crew make sense of what happened. If staff keep raising the same problem and see little change, it can be hard to see the point of speaking up again.

In interviews at one ambulance service in England, staff described feeling that senior managers put pressure on crews to work faster while giving too little attention to their wellbeing. When crews repeatedly flag something that makes it harder to give patients the care they need, managers should look into what’s causing it and tell staff what they’re doing about it.
Support crews feel able to use

Talking to someone they trusted helped people in my interviews make sense of difficult calls. That might be a colleague or someone outside work. In another interview study, paramedics said they wanted time to talk privately after a call, often with the colleague they worked with regularly.

An ambulance service can offer counselling, but staff still have to feel able to use it. Staying composed is often part of caring for a patient in an emergency. If people feel expected to appear unaffected once the call is over, it can be harder to say they’re struggling.

An ambulance service might offer extra support after a major incident. A crew can also reach the end of a shift worn down by a series of calls, even if none on its own would prompt that kind of follow-up.

Training is one place to start. A trial involving 570 student paramedics tested an online programme that taught students how to manage distressing memories and spend less time dwelling on difficult experiences. A year later, students offered the programme were less likely to meet the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder or major depression than those who continued with their usual training.

I’d also like students to hear, before they start taking calls, how the effects of difficult shifts can build up and who they can turn to when that happens. Once crews are on the road, support should feel like part of an ordinary shift. That could mean making time to talk privately after a difficult call.

I see that as part of helping staff develop fortitude. It takes trust to say that a call has got to you, especially when you’re still working out what you need. The way a service responds when someone does speak up can make it easier for the next person to do the same.

articles.title: Duran Duran’s drummer has retired because of tinnitus – here’s why musicians are at higher risk
articles.author: Eldre Beukes, Associate professor, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: After more than 40 years performing with Duran Duran, drummer Roger Taylor has announced he’s retiring because of his worsening tinnitus.

His decision highlights the effect that decades of exposure to loud music can have on musicians and even music lovers. It also illustrates the profound impact tinnitus can have on someone’s relationship with sound and their ability to continue doing something they love.

Tinnitus affects an estimated 740 million adults globally. It’s not actually a disease, but rather a symptom associated with changes in the hearing system and the way the brain processes sound. It is commonly described as a ringing in the ears, though others describe hearing a buzzing, hissing, whistling or humming.

Tinnitus can develop for a number of reasons. One of the most important preventable risk factors for tinnitus and hearing loss is exposure to loud noise. For professional musicians, who are often surrounded by loud or amplified instruments throughout their career, this exposure can accumulate over years of rehearsals, performances and studio recordings.

Research has even found that musicians, whether playing classical, pop or rock music, are more than three times as likely to experience tinnitus as non-musicians. They also face a substantially increased risk of noise-induced hearing loss.
The relationship between sound exposure, hearing damage and tinnitus is complex.

Exposure to excessive sound can damage the delicate sensory structures within the inner ear, contributing to hearing loss and tinnitus. Although symptoms can settle, repeated or intense exposure can permanently damage those cells. Once lost, they cannot grow back and hearing may not recover.

However, risk doesn’t only depend on sound intensity and duration. Factors including previous noise exposure, age, existing hearing loss, genetics and medical conditions such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes, have been linked to an increased risk of both hearing loss and tinnitus.
There’s currently no universally effective treatment or cure for tinnitus. One reason for this is that tinnitus is not a single condition with one underlying cause.

However, the absence of a cure doesn’t mean nothing can be done. There’s a wide range of evidenced-based management options that can significantly reduce tinnitus’s impact on daily life and improve emotional wellbeing and quality of life.
For people who have tinnitus alongside hearing loss, hearing aids can not only improve environmental sounds and communication, but they may also make tinnitus less noticeable.
Some people may find that introducing gentle background sounds, such as music, natural sounds or white noise, makes their tinnitus less noticeable, particularly in quiet environments.

One of the most effective strategies for reducing tinnitus distress is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Rather than attempting to eliminate the tinnitus sound itself, CBT helps people change how they respond to it. This can help provide sustained improvements for the distress, anxiety and poor sleep that tinnitus can cause.

Research is also continuing to advance our understanding of tinnitus, helping drive more personalised approaches to care and aiming to make tinnitus support more accessible through digital technology.
There are also practical steps that musicians and music lovers can take to protect their hearing and lower the risk of developing tinnitus.

High-fidelity or custom-moulded earplugs reduce sound levels while preserving much of the clarity and balance of music. Scheduling regular quiet breaks during rehearsals or gigs, keeping in-ear monitors and headphones at safe levels, increasing distance from loudspeakers and other intense sound sources where possible and avoiding sudden loud sounds, all reduce risks of hearing damage.
Installing acoustic screens, elevating brass and percussion sections, increasing stage spacing and rotating seating during rehearsals can also help reduce musicians’ exposure to loud sound.
Roger Taylor’s decision to step back is a reminder that hearing is one of a musician’s most valuable assets. Protecting it should be an essential part of making and enjoying music.

articles.title: Brain stacking: an expert weighs in on whether this TikTok trend can really boost your brainpower
articles.author: Irene Reppa, Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology, Swansea University
paras: Brain stacking is a new TikTok trend dedicated to making time for activities that engage our mind, such as reading or doing puzzles.

The idea is to allocate specific time to them. People typically “stack” a particular amount of minutes of reading with a specific amount of journalling, for example. That will be followed by stacking a few more minutes of an activity like colouring, and something else like a word search or a sudoku puzzle. But why is this idea considered to be good for the brain? And is there a scientific basis for the idea that engaging in, or combining, activities like these can improve focus, memory or productivity?
If only it was so easy. But maybe there is something useful in brain stacking. Perhaps the more immediate benefit is a sense of wellbeing: joy, happiness or a basic level of contentment.

Let’s unpack what happens when we do some reading at the start of our day. On one level, we purposefully allocate time to ourselves. That can feel good, especially if the rest of the day feels rushed.

Research tracking people in daily life found that, during periods of leisure, they report more positive mood and less stress. That does not prove that a particular morning routine causes these benefits, but it gives us a useful starting point.

Then there is the layer of agency: the feeling that we are the ones deciding what to do. We are not being pushed by someone or something else. Choosing to spend a little time on something we enjoy may be one small way of experiencing that control.

Another thing that can happen when we are involved in an activity is a sense of flow. It involves becoming deeply absorbed in what we are doing, often when the challenge is well matched to our skills. Imagine following a recipe, playing a game or working on a piece of knitting that needs just enough concentration.

With this absorption can come a change in our sense of time. We pay less attention to the clock, so that time can seem to fly. Reading a novel we enjoy can also give us that feeling, even if we would not call every enjoyable reading session a state of flow.

There is another idea behind brain stacking: making room to focus on one task at a time. Multitasking can feel like a necessary evil. But with tasks that demand our conscious attention, what we call multitasking often involves switching between them.

Some activities can be done together, such as walking and talking, particularly when they are familiar and relatively undemanding. The difficulty comes when tasks compete for the same limited resources. Switching takes time, so performance can suffer. We may feel we are doing everything at once, but important parts of the processing are taking turns.

How might brain stacking help, then? By giving us a period with fewer competing demands and interruptions. That is a plausible benefit, rather than evidence that the routine resets the brain or removes stress at a neural level. And if we are already absorbed in our book, we do not need to stop after five minutes just to move on to the next item in the stack.
A useful question is how the activity fits into our lives. Do we enjoy it? Can we choose when to stop? Does it leave room for sleep, other interests and the people around us?

Like trends in general, this one has attracted exaggerated claims. Evidence about leisure, attention and practice does not establish that stacking particular hobbies improves memory, focus or productivity more generally. Getting better at a puzzle is also different from improving our ability to think and remember across everyday life. Research on brain training makes this distinction clear: improvements on the practised task do not necessarily translate into broad improvements elsewhere.

There is also an assumption behind some of these claims: that our focus, memory and productivity all need to be improved. For many of us, a hobby does not need to be justified as a way of making our brain work harder or better. Enjoying it can be reason enough.

If you want to try brain stacking, start with something you already enjoy. Give yourself some uninterrupted time. There is no evidence-based requirement to complete a certain number of hobbies, or to spend a particular number of minutes on each. And do not turn it into another thing to be good at. If it starts to feel like homework, something has probably been lost along the way.

So, yes, do go ahead and brain stack as long as you do not lose sleep or money over it, or force yourself into activities you do not enjoy. Good nutrition, sufficient sleep and a circle of friends and family are important too. Those are not trends, not yet at least.
