articles.title: ‘Spermmaxxing’ promises better fertility, but the evidence is thin
articles.author: Michael Carroll, Reader  / Associate Professor in Reproductive Science, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: Shining red light on your testicles or sitting in a sauna with an ice pack: social media has plenty of unusual suggestions for improving sperm quality.

This trend, sometimes called “spermmaxxing”, encourages men to take control of their reproductive health. As a reproductive scientist, I welcome that interest – I’ve even written a book about it. Male fertility has historically received less attention than women’s, and many men know surprisingly little about how their own bodies work.
But some spermmaxxing advice is based on experiments that tell us very little about someone’s actual chances of having a baby.
Listen to Michael Carroll speak about spermmaxxing on The Conversation Weekly podcast and on the Strange Health podcast.

A sperm count is only part of the picture. When scientists analyse semen, the fluid released during ejaculation, we examine how many sperm it contains, how many are alive and how well they swim. Their ability to move forwards is called progressive motility.

The World Health Organization’s reference figures include 39 million sperm per ejaculate and 30% moving forwards. These figures represent the lower end of results recorded among men whose partners conceived within a year. They are not a pass-or-fail fertility test.
Someone with a low sperm count may still conceive, while someone with millions of apparently healthy sperm may struggle. Pregnancy also depends on the egg and other stages of reproduction.
And, as my own research has shown, sperm can swim normally while carrying DNA damage that a routine test misses.
Do spermmaxxing hacks work?
Take red-light therapy. A laboratory study found that exposing sperm to particular wavelengths of red or near-infrared light improved their movement.
But shining light on sperm in a laboratory dish is very different from shining it on someone’s testicles. There is insufficient evidence that doing so improves fertility.
Then there are ice packs, sometimes promoted for use in saunas.

The testicles hang outside the body because sperm production works best at temperatures 2-4°C below normal body temperature. Research involving ten men found that regular sauna exposure temporarily impaired sperm production.

But putting ice against the scrotum, the pouch of skin containing the testicles, is not an established fertility treatment and risks injuring the skin. Avoiding prolonged excessive heat is a more sensible approach.
Abstinence advice is equally confusing. Some influencers suggest saving up sperm by avoiding ejaculation for long periods.

Longer gaps can increase the number of sperm in a sample, but an analysis of 13 clinical trials found that shorter periods of abstinence were associated with better forward movement and less DNA fragmentation – breaks in the genetic material carried by sperm.

This doesn’t mean ejaculating as frequently as possible will improve fertility. The optimal interval remains uncertain, and a change in sperm measurements does not necessarily translate into a greater chance of pregnancy.
Another misconception is that taking testosterone will help you produce more sperm.

The hormone is essential for sperm production, but taking testosterone supplements or anabolic steroids can suppress the signals from the brain telling the testicles to produce their own testosterone.
This can dramatically reduce sperm production, sometimes to zero. Production often recovers after treatment stops, but recovery can take months or longer.
Men considering testosterone treatment who want children should discuss fertility with their doctor beforehand.
What a sperm test can miss
Sperm need to carry healthy DNA, the genetic instructions passed from a father to a developing embryo.
In research my colleagues and I conducted, we exposed human sperm in the laboratory to compounds involved in glycation, chemical reactions between sugars and protein molecules.
One compound, glyoxal, increased a marker of oxidative DNA damage without significantly affecting how well the sperm swam.
This experiment does not prove that eating sugar causes infertility. It demonstrates why sperm counts and swimming ability cannot tell us everything about reproductive health.
And what about alarming claims that sperm counts are collapsing worldwide?
A large analysis published in 2023 reported substantial declines across studies spanning several decades.
However, a 2026 Danish study involving 8,320 men found relatively stable semen measurements between 1996 and 2022.

These studies examined different populations using different methods. The Danish findings do not disprove declines elsewhere, but they demonstrate why we need to examine geographical differences and study methods before drawing sweeping conclusions about global fertility.
There is more reason to focus on general health than expensive fertility gadgets.
Smoking is associated with poorer semen quality. Research has also linked vaping with lower sperm counts, although it cannot establish that vaping carries the same reproductive risks as smoking.

A 2025 review found associations between Mediterranean-style diets, rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and olive oil, and some measures of better sperm quality. However, stronger evidence is needed to establish whether following this diet improves pregnancy rates.

Research also links disrupted sleep with poorer sperm quality. Exercise and maintaining a healthy weight can support reproductive health, although lifestyle changes cannot resolve every cause of infertility.
If conception is proving difficult, both partners should be assessed. The NHS recommends seeking medical advice after a year of trying, or sooner in certain circumstances.
Finally, sperm count is no measure of masculinity. Men experiencing infertility can face considerable isolation and shame, and turning sperm production into a competition risks making that worse.

Greater interest in male fertility is welcome. But improving reproductive health requires understanding what the science can tell us, recognising what remains uncertain and giving men access to reliable information rather than another miracle cure.

articles.title: Most children labelled allergic to antibiotics may not have an allergy, researchers warn
articles.author: Rebecca Payne, Clinical Senior Lecturer, Bangor University; University of Oxford
paras: It’s seven o’clock on a Saturday night in an urgent care centre. A ten-year-old boy is “proper poorly” with severe tonsillitis and clearly needs antibiotics. Just before I (Rebecca Payne) head out to find a suitable medicine, I ask his mother: “Does he have any allergies?”
“Yes,” she says. “He can’t have penicillin or anything ending in -mycin.”

Finding the right treatment is going to be difficult. Penicillin and clarithromicin are the first-choice antibiotics for tonsillitis, and the alternatives are not recommended as first-line treatments. With an unwell child and a worried mother, this is not the ideal moment to investigate an allergy history that goes back years.

This scenario is a surprisingly common problem. Around one in 20 children in the US has a penicillin allergy recorded in their medical notes. Yet research suggests most children labelled as allergic to penicillin are not truly allergic.

In our recent article in the British Journal of General Practice, we explain how GPs can identify children who may have been wrongly labelled as allergic and remove inaccurate entries from their medical records. A structured conversation with families about what happened when the allergy was first recorded can help establish whether the child really had an allergic reaction.

Many childhood antibiotic allergy labels begin during viral infections. Viruses can cause rashes that appear while a child is taking antibiotics. Parents and doctors may assume the medicine caused the rash, when the real cause was the virus. Vomiting, headaches, fever and joint pain can also be mistaken for signs of an allergy.
Once an allergy is added to a child’s medical records, it can be difficult to remove. The label may follow them into adulthood, even if they were never allergic in the first place.

This is important because it means children risk receiving antibiotics which are less effective and which kill off a much wider range of bacteria than required. This puts them at risk of infection by superbugs like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and other pathogens like C difficile. The consequences can include longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs.

But there is a way to address the problem. Removing an incorrect allergy label from someone’s medical records is known as “de-labelling”. Our recent article outlines how GPs can work with families to establish what actually happened when a child was first labelled allergic.

UK guidance already provides a framework for removing inaccurate penicillin allergy labels in hospitals. Research has also shown that a structured approach can work safely in outpatient clinics and primary care. In that 2024 study, 91% of the children assessed had their allergy labels removed.
A careful conversation can help GPs place children into three groups, depending on their symptoms and medical history.

The first group includes children whose original symptoms were never typical of an allergy, those who have since taken the same antibiotic without problems and those labelled allergic simply because another family member has an allergy. In these cases, the label can be removed without further tests or a specialist referral. Families can then be reassured that their child can take the medicine.

The second group includes children who developed a mild rash but had no serious symptoms, such as breathing difficulties or feeling faint. After a careful assessment, a doctor can prescribe a single dose of the antibiotic for the child to take at home. The family is then contacted after a week to check for any reaction. If there has been no reaction, the allergy label can be removed. This approach must be overseen by a professional such as a GP or practice pharmacist. Parents should never try giving their child an antibiotic again without medical advice.

The third group includes children who have had a severe reaction, such as anaphylaxis or a serious rash affecting the mouth or other moist areas of the body. Children with severe or poorly controlled asthma may also need specialist assessment. These children should be referred to a paediatric allergy or immunology service. It is vital that children with a genuine allergy are not given the medicine that caused it.

Keeping an uncertain allergy label can feel like the safest option for both parents and healthcare professionals. But leaving an incorrect label in place carries risks too. Reviewing it can help families understand which medicines their child can safely take and allow doctors to choose the most appropriate treatment when they become ill. Reducing unnecessary use of broader-spectrum antibiotics also helps tackle antibiotic resistance, which contributes to keeping these medicines effective for everyone.

If your child has been told they are allergic to an antibiotic, ask your GP whether the diagnosis could be reviewed, ideally when they are well. If the label is removed, you should receive a clear explanation and written confirmation. The change should also be shared with other relevant healthcare professionals. That way, an assumption made years earlier is less likely to dictate a child’s future treatment.

articles.title: Your brain may be hiding Alzheimer’s from you – and that’s not always a good thing
articles.author: Eleftheria Kodosaki, Research Fellow in Neuroimmunology, UCL
paras: When scientists examine the brains of older people after death, what they find can often be puzzling. One such puzzle is that around a third of people who showed no signs of dementia when they were alive, had brains which contained key indicators of Alzheimer’s disease.
Neuroscientists describe these people as being “resilient” to Alzheimer’s. They see this trait as a good thing, and have spent decades trying to understand what makes a brain resilient.
The hope is that if we can find out, we may then be able to protect more people from the disease.
But coping with a disease isn’t the same as being protected from it. A brain that copes well may also be hiding the disease – sometimes until it’s too late to act.

Alzheimer’s disease unfolds in stages. First, proteins called amyloid and tau build up in the brain as plaques and clumps known as “tangles”. Then the brain cells (neurons) are damaged and die. Finally, memory and thinking begin to fail.
Some people never accumulate much amyloid or tau despite having a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers call this “resistance”.
Others experience a build up of amyloid and tau, but cope with it. This is resilience.
There are two key forms of resilience. In the first, someone may have plenty of amyloid and tau in the brain but they don’t lose many brain cells.

In the second form, this amyloid and tau build-up does result in the loss of brain cells – but the person may still continue thinking clearly. Or, if there is cognitive decline, it’s very slow – so symptoms are less noticeable.
This second form of resilience should worry us most, because a person can seem perfectly well while their brain is quietly shrinking.

This situation is often seen in women. On average, women have better verbal memory than men throughout life, meaning they have better recall of language-based information such as words, names and stories.

But this can be a problem when identifying Alzheimer’s, as the memory tests used to diagnose the disease rely heavily on verbal memory. Research has even found that women with signs of Alzheimer’s scored better on memory tests than men who had similar signs of the disease.

A similar pattern is also seen in people with high “cognitive reserve”. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to adapt and improvise when it faces a setback – such as those caused by ageing or disease. Cognitive reserve is built throughout life by things such as education and mentally demanding work.

People with high cognitive reserve tend to develop Alzheimer’s symptoms later. But once symptoms do appear, brain function tends to decline more quickly. This is usually because by the time symptoms develop the disease is already quite far along.

So although resilience can protect a person’s cognitive health for years, the disease eventually outpaces the brain’s ability to cope. The resilience that was once beneficial to us is suddenly no longer helpful.
This can be a problem for several reasons.
The first problem is that it can delay diagnosis. This means a person won’t get the support they need at a crucial stage.

Another problem with resilience is that if it hides the disease until it’s in its advanced stages, people may miss the window for when treatment could help most. The only drugs currently approved to slow the progression of Alzheimer’s must be taken in the early stages of the disease to potentially have any effect.

Resilience can also make it difficult when researching and testing new Alzheimer’s drugs. People who cope well decline slowly overall – whether they receive a drug or a placebo. This could make a drug look weaker or stronger than it might actually be. It may also be one of the reasons why a drug may not work equally well for all people who have Alzheimer’s disease.

For example, one Alzheimer’s drug was found to be more effective in people who were less resilient. For people who were highly resilient (even though they had high levels of tau in their brain and similar cognition as the less resilient people), there wasn’t a clear benefit.
There’s still much scientists don’t know about resilience.
Although genetics can provide some information about a person’s Alzheimer’s risk and the disease’s likely progression, it unfortunately can’t tell us very much about resilience.
We still need to figure out what’s happening in the brains of people who stay well, and what exactly changes in the brain when that protection starts to fail.

But ongoing research may help us answer these questions someday. Biomarkers, which are measurable signs of a disease, can detect Alzheimer’s from a blood sample. If paired with a cognitive test, this could let researchers see how much disease a person carries, how much damage it’s doing and how well a person’s cognitive function has held up.
Biomarkers could also improve research for treatments by showing which interventions really have an effect in slowing the disease or making people resilient or even resistant.

When it comes to Alzheimer’s, resilience shows us that carrying the disease doesn’t have to mean losing your memory or your independence. But it can also hide signs of the disease until it’s too late.
Uncovering the biology behind resilience could allow us to offer protection to those who need it – and intervene earlier for those who are highly resilient.

articles.title: 300 years after the woman who ‘gave birth to rabbits’: why the legendary hoax still matters
articles.author: Karen Harvey, Professor of Cultural History, University of Birmingham
paras: The portrait of Mary Toft is innocuous enough. But the sitter’s firm grip on the rabbit in her lap is the clue to the extraordinary story it depicts. Toft’s distinction was to be the only woman, as far as I know, to have claimed to give birth to rabbits.
Three hundred years on, and as I discuss in my book, The Imposteress Rabbit Breeder, the questions raised by this case continue to resonate.

You may be familiar with these rabbit births. Hilary Mantel referred to them in her 1998 historical novel The Giant, O'Brien. They were also obliquely referenced in the 2018 film The Favourite, about Britain’s Queen Anne. If you had lived within reach of English news or gossip in 1726, you would almost certainly have heard the story.

Toft was 23 and living in Guildford, Surrey, when she supposedly started giving birth to rabbits that September. Soon, major British newspapers were devoting front-page column inches to the affair. The fullest account was delivered to readers in the Daily Journal on Monday November 14, when it reported that “a poor Woman” had been “delivered by Mr. John Howard, an eminent Surgeon and Man-Midwife living at Guildford, of a Creature resembling a Rabbit”.

In 1726, Toft was asked for her own account of the rabbit births. She explained that she and her fellow workers had chased a rabbit in a field. Unable to catch it, she had been plagued by thoughts of rabbits night and day.

Her explanation drew on a medical theory known as the maternal imagination: the belief that a pregnant woman’s thoughts and experiences could physically shape her unborn child. Toft, or someone close to her, evidently knew enough about this theory to make her story seem plausible.

But, and no surprises here, the rabbit births were a hoax. In the end, a porter at the London establishment where Toft was being kept reported that rabbits had been smuggled into the building. The game was up.

A poor woman who could not read or write had apparently hoodwinked members of the medical establishment, including doctors connected to King George I’s court. In this deeply unequal and patriarchal society, Toft was a profoundly unsettling figure. As my research suggests, the response to the hoax was shaped by wider anxieties about social disorder and the behaviour of the poor.
After interrogation, Toft confessed and blamed the affair on her mother-in-law, as recorded in her final surviving statement of December 1726.

But people had largely stopped listening. She was presented as somewhat incidental to the events at the time, as you can see from the following contemporary satirical engraving by William Hogarth: doctors crowd around Toft’s bed, examining the supposed births while the woman herself lies almost forgotten at the edge of the scene. Historians have often taken a similar approach, focusing on the gullibility of the doctors or the scandal that engulfed them.
Centring women’s experience

My study of Toft’s accounts) instead places her experiences at the centre of the story. Her three surviving statements, although recorded under interrogation, offer a window into her social and emotional world.

Toft described two sets of events. The first was a difficult miscarriage. Her moving and visceral descriptions of pain and prolonged bleeding provide a rare historical account of early pregnancy loss.

The second was the hoax itself. Again, the details of Toft’s experiences are graphic. Animal parts were placed inside her body and subsequently removed during supposed deliveries. For all the written and visual satire the case produced, the hoax involved a real and potentially dangerous physical ordeal.

Toft repeatedly described being surrounded by women. At first, they were supportive, but in her telling they became increasingly menacing. She accused them of abusing their power and forcing her to perform the role of rabbit-breeder, risking her health and liberty.
Perhaps they were punishing her for the miscarriage. Perhaps they hoped to make money from this curious spectacle. Or perhaps Toft’s account was shaped by her desperation to escape punishment.

Toft’s descriptions of pain and bleeding give us a rare account of what miscarriage felt like to a woman in the 18th century. In maternity care today, how staff respond when a woman describes her pain can affect when she’s examined or offered pain relief. In England’s 2025 maternity survey, almost one in five respondents who raised a concern during labour or birth felt it hadn’t been taken seriously. Some described asking for pain relief and feeling that staff didn’t believe how much pain they were in. As one respondent put it, “I feel my contractions were not taken seriously during my induction.”

The doctors who examined Toft left a record of what they thought they saw. Her own statements give us an account of what she felt and what she said others did to her. Taking those statements seriously brings us closer to understanding what happened to her.

articles.title: Acupuncture-like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
articles.author: Flis Bishop, Professor of Health Psychology, University of Southampton
paras: A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.
Women who received the treatment lost about 2kg more, on average, than those given a sham treatment after 12 weeks. By 24 weeks, the difference had grown to about 3kg.
The technique is called acupoint thread embedding. Acupuncturists use fine needles to insert absorbable threads into chosen points on the body.

They check that the points are being stimulated by looking for a particular needle sensation, known as de qi. The 1–2cm threads then dissolve over several weeks. Until they do, they keep stimulating the points.
In standard acupuncture, needles go into the same points and produce the same sensation. But they come out at the end of each session.
That means thread embedding may have longer-lasting effects. It could also mean fewer, less frequent treatments for patients, although the study didn’t test for these things.
The study was published in the Annals of Internal Medicine. It randomly assigned 132 women to either the real treatment or a sham one.
Experienced acupuncturists, specially trained for the study, gave six sessions over 12 weeks. The threads were made of a biodegradable material called polydioxanone. They were inserted 2–4cm deep.

The sham treatment took place in the same setting. The same acupuncturists used the same type of needles at the same points. But the needles went in only 1cm, so the de qi sensation – an aching or tingling – was not triggered and no threads were used.

This allowed the researchers to rule out other explanations. These include light stimulation of the points, the practitioner–patient relationship and patients’ expectations, known as the placebo effect.
It seems to have been convincing. The women did not know which treatment they had received. So the difference in results can be put down to the threads.
The staff measuring the results and the statisticians didn’t know either, which helps to reduce bias.

Women were measured at the start, at 12 weeks (the end of treatment) and at 24 weeks. Researchers tracked weight, body mass index (BMI), waist and hip size, body fat, heart and metabolic health, and self-reported measures such as appetite.

As well as losing 2–3kg more, women who had the real treatment saw bigger drops in BMI, waist and hip size, body fat and self-reported appetite. Together, these give a fuller picture, because several measures are needed to judge weight-related health.

Some measures changed similarly in both groups. Compared with the sham treatment, the threads made no difference to cholesterol or fasting blood sugar. Nor did they affect anxiety, wellbeing or weight-related quality of life.
Side-effects such as bruising or pain at acupuncture points and the number of women leaving the study were also similar in both groups. But larger studies are needed to spot rare side-effects.

The researchers reached their planned number of participants. But 132 women was too few to test whether the treatment works differently in different groups. For example, does it work better for women who start at a higher weight?

The women were Chinese, aged 18 to 45, generally healthy, and were overweight with a BMI of at least 24 at the start. While in the UK a BMI of at least 25 is considered overweight, in China a BMI of 24 counts as overweight because the effect of BMI on health varies by ethnicity.
The study cannot say what the threads do for men, women over 45 or under-18s.
It also cannot say how the threads led to weight loss. Women who had them reported a bigger drop in appetite. That suggests changes in eating habits might partly explain the result.
But the researchers didn’t measure food intake or energy burned. So we don’t know whether a smaller appetite meant eating less, or whether something else was going on.
The weight loss lasted for 12 weeks after the 12-week course ended. But, as many people know from experience, losing weight is hard and keeping it off is harder.

Most people regain weight in the months and years after behaviour-change programmes, weight-loss drugs and other treatments. People who lose more weight tend to regain more, and faster. Regular support from health professionals can soften this. Thread embedding may offer a new approach to this problem.
Larger studies should test other groups of people and look at longer periods. They should also check whether top-up treatments are needed.
They should also compare the costs and benefits with treatments recommended in official guidelines.
The answers could help health services decide whether to offer acupoint thread embedding.

articles.title: Young Americans have no memory of AIDS at its worst – they’re still at risk of infection, even when HIV doesn’t feel like a threat
articles.author: Andrés Henao, Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: For Americans who came of age in the 1980s and early 1990s, HIV/AIDS was difficult to ignore. Hospitals were filled with young people sick with infections and cancers rarely seen in healthy adults. Friends and partners were quickly dying. Public health officials warned that the disease, primarily transmitted through sexual contact or sharing drug needles, had no effective treatment.

At the height of the U.S. epidemic in 1995, more than 56,000 people with AIDS died in a single year. Then antiretroviral therapy – medications that stop HIV from multiplying – transformed the epidemic. Over the next three years, AIDS diagnoses fell by 45%, while deaths among people with AIDS fell 63%.

Someone who is 20 years old today was born into a very different world. HIV is now a manageable chronic infection for people who can access and remain on treatment. As of 2025, over 20% of people around the world with HIV were unable to access treatment. As an infectious diseases physician caring for people with HIV, I have watched that transformation change not only the lives of my patients, but also the way people think about this once fatal disease.
That success raises an unusual public health question: How do you prevent new infections in a generation that grew up with no memory of a disease at its worst?
The change in life expectancy with HIV since the 1980s has been extraordinary.

Modern antiretroviral treatment can reduce the amount of HIV in the blood to levels that standard tests cannot detect. People who maintain this viral suppression can live long, healthy lives. Just as importantly, a person with a sustained undetectable viral load won’t sexually transmit HIV – a principle known as undetectable equals untransmittable, or U=U.

People without HIV also now have highly effective prevention options. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, can dramatically reduce the risk of acquiring HIV. Initially available as a daily pill, PrEP has since expanded to longer-lasting options. In 2021, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved an injectable drug called cabotegravir that is administered every other month to prevent HIV infection. In 2025, the FDA approved an injectable drug called lenacapavir for HIV prevention, which only requires administration once every six months.
But HIV has not disappeared.
In 2024, 38,793 people were diagnosed with HIV in the U.S. and several territories. People ages 25 to 34 accounted for 37% of those diagnoses – the largest share of any age group.

In 2025, about 26 million of the 41 million people living with HIV around the world were in sub-Saharan Africa. More than 20 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment – an extraordinary expansion of treatment access compared with the early decades of the epidemic.
However, the dismantling of U.S. global aid during the second Trump administration has disrupted the community programs and delivery systems that make sustained HIV treatment possible.
When success makes a disease less visible
Public health sometimes faces a paradox: Successful prevention efforts can make a disease seem less threatening than it still is.

Measles offers a useful, though imperfect, comparison. Before vaccines became available, measles infected millions of Americans and caused hundreds of deaths each year. Vaccination eventually made the disease so uncommon that in 2000, the United States declared measles eliminated in the country.

Yet measles didn’t stop being dangerous. When vaccination rates fall, the virus can return. In 2026, the United States has seen thousands of new measles cases, overwhelmingly among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. Declining vaccination rates – fueled in part by persistent misinformation and vaccine skepticism – have allowed measles to regain a foothold. On Nov. 13, 2026, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status.

HIV is very different from measles: It does not spread through respiratory droplets, and there is still no effective HIV vaccine. But the two diseases illustrate a similar challenge: When people no longer regularly witness the consequences of an infection, the reason for preventing it can become less intuitive.

Thanks to medical advances, younger adults view HIV differently from their parents’ generation. The AIDS wards, funeral notices and intense public campaigns of the early epidemic are in history rather than in memory. That generational distance may matter for public health. A 2026 national survey found that only 31% of Gen Z adults said they felt knowledgeable about HIV, compared with 60% of Gen X adults who came of age during the height of the AIDS epidemic.
Accessing HIV prevention tools

It would be too simplistic to say that young people have become complacent only because they no longer fear AIDS. Access to health care, stigma, education and new prevention tools all influence a person’s risk of contracting HIV.

Condoms remain an important HIV prevention tool: When used correctly and consistently, condoms are highly effective at reducing sexual transmission of HIV. But in a study of over 13,500 sexually active U.S. high school students, less than 60% reported in 2013 that they used a condom the last time they had sex. By 2023, that figure declined to 52%. Only 7% of all high school students reported ever having been tested for HIV.

At the same time, the availability of highly effective preventive medication does not mean everyone who could benefit is using it. HIV testing programs funded by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that only a little over 57% of people tested in nonhealthcare settings had heard of PrEP. Less than 9% of those with a negative HIV test were currently taking PrEP.

Younger people have also lagged behind older groups in PrEP use. An analysis of a federally run national HIV database found that less than 24% of people ages 13 to 24 who could benefit from PrEP were prescribed it in 2022, compared with over 45% of those ages 35 to 44.
These gaps indicate that having powerful prevention tools is not the same as getting them to the people who need them.
A new message for HIV prevention

HIV in 2026 is not HIV in 1986. Recreating the fear people felt about AIDS in the 1980s is neither realistic nor desirable. Fear came with enormous stigma against gay men, people who inject drugs and people living with HIV – stigma still stubbornly persists today.

Current U.S. HIV prevention campaigns emphasize reducing stigma and often tailor messages to communities disproportionately affected by HIV. But gaps remain in reaching people who do not see themselves as at risk: In 2025, only 34% of sexually active straight adults at increased risk for HIV had heard of PrEP, and just 1% were using it.
Prevention messages for younger generations instead can reflect what decades of scientific advances have made possible: HIV prevention and the ability to live fully with HIV.

There are still substantial gaps in understanding about HIV treatment and prevention, especially among teens and young adults. Although HIV infection is now treatable and manageable across large swathes of the globe, it still requires regular medical monitoring and treatment. Understanding that effective treatment prevents sexual transmission can fight stigma without suggesting that acquiring HIV has no consequences.

Time travel isn’t necessary to witness some of the devastation that HIV can cause. Access to treatment remains unequal. Some pockets of the U.S. and the poorest regions of the globe still experience AIDS-related complications and opportunistic infections. HIV infection may also lead to a slightly lower life expectancy due to an increased risk of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

World AIDS Day on Dec. 1 is partly an opportunity to remember the millions of people lost during an epidemic that transformed medicine, public health and entire communities. Preserving that history is not about asking today’s young people to inherit an earlier generation’s fear. The greater challenge is making sure they inherit its lessons – while giving them the far better tools for prevention that earlier generations never had.

articles.title: Five things that shape body weight – by an obesity expert
articles.author: Thomas Barber, Associate Professor and Honorary Consultant Endocrinologist, University of Warwick
paras: What you eat when you’re tired and hungry might come down to what’s open on the way home and what you can afford. Both appetite and access to food shape decisions that can look, from the outside, like simple matters of choice.

The World Health Organization describes obesity as a chronic disease shaped by the interaction between biology and the conditions people live in. In my new book, Obesity: Life Beyond the GLP-1 Injection, I look at what shapes body weight and what that means for treatment and prevention. Here are five findings that informed the book.
1. Losing weight can make you hungrier

In one study, adults who lost weight on a very low-calorie diet still reported feeling hungrier a year after the diet ended than they had before it began. Their levels of leptin, a hormone that helps tell the brain how much energy the body has stored, were still lower than before the diet.

A lighter body takes less energy to maintain and move. A review of studies found that energy use can sometimes fall even further than you’d expect for a person’s new weight. This extra drop tended to be smaller in better-designed studies and could fade once weight stabilised.

That leaves some people trying to manage stronger feelings of hunger at a time when their bodies need fewer calories. It helps explain why keeping weight off can be difficult even when someone is still making a deliberate effort.
2. Genes influence appetite

Some of the differences in body weight between people come from the genes they inherit. In rare cases, a change in a single gene can cause severe obesity in early childhood. More often, many genetic differences each contribute a little. Studies of both patterns point to the parts of the brain involved in appetite, which helps explain why some people may feel full sooner than others.

In a Norwegian study, researchers used DNA to group people by their inherited tendency to have a higher body mass index, or BMI, a measure of weight relative to height. Over several decades, average BMI rose across the groups, with a bigger rise among those with the strongest genetic tendency.
The rise across groups points to changes in the conditions people lived in. The bigger rise in some groups suggests that the same changes can affect people differently.
3. Sleeping less can make you eat more
A review of experiments found that people tended to eat more when their sleep was cut short. There was much less evidence that cutting sleep changed how many calories they burned.

Researchers then tested what happened when people who usually slept less than six and a half hours a night got more sleep. In a two-week trial of 80 adults with overweight, one group received advice tailored to their sleep habits and the other kept its usual routine.

Those given advice slept about an hour longer and took in about 270 fewer calories a day, on average, compared with the other group. Both groups were free to choose what they ate. Whether the difference in calorie intake lasts is still unclear, and keeping regular sleep hours can be difficult for people who work nights or care for someone.
4. Semaglutide can lower the risk of serious heart problems and stroke
Semaglutide mimics GLP-1, a hormone that helps regulate appetite. The medicine can help people feel fuller and less hungry.

In a large trial of adults with existing heart or circulation problems and overweight or obesity, none of whom had diabetes, researchers compared semaglutide with a placebo, an injection with no active drug. Over an average of just over three years, 65 in every 1,000 people on semaglutide died from cardiovascular causes or had a non-fatal heart attack or stroke, compared with 80 in every 1,000 on the placebo. About 17 in every 100 people taking semaglutide stopped because of side effects, compared with eight in every 100 taking the placebo.

A separate study followed people for a year after their semaglutide and lifestyle support ended. On average, they regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost. People who stop taking the medicine may still need support to manage their weight.
5. Food policy can change what’s on offer

In a hospital study, the same 20 adults spent two weeks on a diet high in ultra-processed foods and two weeks on a diet based on unprocessed foods. They could eat as much or as little as they wanted. They ate about 500 more calories a day on the ultra-processed diet and ate those meals faster. Eating speed is one possible explanation for the difference, and the study shows how much the food on offer can affect what people eat even when they decide their own portions.

The UK’s soft drinks levy gave manufacturers a reason to change their recipes: using less sugar could reduce or avoid the charge. An analysis of English school measurements found that after the levy came into effect, there were about 16 fewer cases of obesity per 1,000 girls aged 10 and 11 than researchers would have expected if earlier trends had continued. Researchers found no overall reduction among boys of the same age or among children aged four and five. But other changes around the same time could have contributed to the result.

People living with obesity need access to effective treatment and long-term support. Governments can also help prevent obesity by changing how foods are made and marketed and by making nutritious food more affordable in the places people already shop.

articles.title: Sperm counts may be falling, but humans are unlikely to run out
articles.author: Michael Carroll, Reader  / Associate Professor in Reproductive Science, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: For years, alarming headlines have warned that sperm counts are plummeting and humanity could be heading towards a fertility crisis. But new research suggests the picture is considerably more complicated.

A study published in September 2026 examined semen samples from 8,320 young Danish men collected over 26 years. Rather than finding a steady decline, the researchers reported that sperm counts had remained relatively stable between 1996 and 2022, with some modest improvements in recent years.
That doesn’t mean everything is fine. More than a third of the men had at least one measure of semen quality below World Health Organization reference levels.

These findings contrast with an influential 2017 study reporting that sperm concentration among men in Western countries had fallen by more than half between 1973 and 2011. When the researchers expanded their analysis in 2022, they concluded that sperm counts were declining worldwide, with the rate of decline accelerating.

As a reproductive scientist specialising in sperm biology and male fertility, I’ve spent much of my career studying how sperm function and what influences their quality. In my book, Your Nuts: The Science of How They Work and What It Means for Your Fertility, I explore what sperm counts can tell us about reproductive health, and more importantly, what they cannot

So what is actually happening to human sperm numbers? Are they falling worldwide, or do trends differ between populations? And perhaps most importantly, what do sperm counts really tell us about male fertility?
Are sperm counts still falling?
While the results from the 2017 study appear alarming, more recent studies have continued to produce very different results.

A review published online in 2024 analysed research involving almost 12,000 US men. Its main analyses found no statistically significant decline in sperm concentration between 1970 and 2018. However, a modest decline emerged when researchers adjusted for both geographical region and fertility status.

Another 2024 study examined semen samples from prospective sperm donors in Denmark. Sperm concentration and total sperm count remained relatively stable between 2017 and 2022, although sperm motility, or how well sperm move, declined.

Between 2019 and 2022, the concentration of moving sperm fell by 16%, while the total number of moving sperm per ejaculate declined by 22%. This is important because sperm movement is another factor influencing the likelihood of conception.

Meanwhile, researchers in Ireland analysed more than 18,000 semen samples from over 15,000 men attending a fertility clinic between 2008 and 2023. They found that median sperm concentration increased by almost 23%, from 57 million to 70 million sperm per millilitre. However, the proportion of samples containing very low concentrations of sperm, or no sperm at all, remained relatively unchanged.

Taken together, these studies suggest that trends in semen quality can vary considerably between populations and regions. And this means that the question of whether sperm counts are declining globally is far from settled.

There are also important limitations. Studies involving sperm donors or fertility clinic patients may not reflect the wider population. Meanwhile, research examining long-term trends often relies on semen samples collected at different times and locations, sometimes using different methods.
These differences make comparisons difficult. The newer studies cannot simply cancel out the larger global analyses, but they demonstrate why interpreting changes in sperm counts requires caution.
Sperm count isn’t the same as fertility
There is another problem with the extinction narrative: sperm count alone cannot tell us whether a man is fertile.

Semen analysis also considers sperm movement and shape, alongside other characteristics. Although very low sperm concentrations can reduce the likelihood of conception, they do not necessarily make pregnancy impossible.

Research into male contraception illustrates this. In trials of hormonal contraceptives, pregnancies occurred even when sperm concentrations had been suppressed to very low levels, including three million sperm per millilitre or less. Although the likelihood of conception was greatly reduced, it was not eliminated.
This demonstrates why sperm numbers cannot be treated as a simple dividing line between fertility and infertility.
There is also enormous natural variation in the number of sperm an individual man produces, including differences between samples collected from the same person.

In one study involving 329 men, researchers found considerable variation in semen measurements over time. Relying on a single sample could sometimes give a misleading picture of an individual’s semen quality.
This is one reason current UK clinical guidance recommends repeat semen analysis when an initial result is abnormal.

It also illustrates the difficulty of determining whether sperm counts have fallen over several decades, particularly when the studies involved different populations and methods of collecting and analysing samples.
None of this means we should dismiss concerns about male reproductive health.

Male infertility is a significant health issue, and research into the environmental, lifestyle and medical factors that influence sperm production remains important. As the World Health Organization acknowledges, infertility affects millions of people worldwide, and male reproductive health deserves greater attention.
But the evidence doesn’t support the idea that humanity is about to disappear because we’re running out of sperm.
The dramatic headlines may have overstated the science. What they achieved, however, was to shine a much-needed light on male fertility, and that is a conversation worth having.

articles.title: Scientists find way to repair heart damage after a heart attack
articles.author: David C. Gaze, Senior Lecturer in Chemical Pathology, University of Westminster
paras: Every year, millions of people worldwide suffer a heart attack. Thanks to advances in emergency treatment, many now survive an event that might once have been fatal. Yet surviving a heart attack is not necessarily the end of the story. The damage can be permanent, increasing the risk of heart failure, breathlessness and a poorer quality of life.

Researchers have developed an experimental treatment that could change how we approach recovery after a heart attack. Rather than simply protecting the remaining heart muscle, the new approach aims to encourage the heart to repair itself. So far, it has only been tested in mice.

The findings, published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research, describe how modified messenger RNA (mRNA) can encourage heart muscle cells to multiply, potentially improving the heart’s ability to pump blood.
Although this is still early-stage research, the study offers the tantalising possibility that one day we might be able to encourage the adult human heart to regenerate damaged muscle.
Why the heart struggles to repair itself

A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow through a coronary artery is significantly reduced or even fully blocked. Without oxygen, the cells of the heart muscle begin to die. These specialised cells, called cardiomyocytes, are responsible for the continuous contractions of the heart muscle, which pumps blood around the body to our vital organs.

Unlike skin or liver tissue, the adult human heart has limited capacity to replace damaged cells. Instead, dead muscle is largely replaced by fibrous scar tissue. Although this scar helps maintain the heart’s structural integrity, it cannot contract like healthy muscle.
The consequence is a heart that may become progressively weaker, sometimes leading to heart failure.

Modern treatments, such as procedures to reopen blocked arteries, medication and supervised exercise programmes, have greatly improved survival. But they cannot replace heart muscle that has already died.

During the early development of the heart, the cardiomyocytes divide, allowing the heart muscle to grow. Shortly after birth, most mammalian cardiomyocytes largely lose this ability. The researchers investigated whether they could restart this process by making heart muscle cells produce two proteins, called Myc and cyclin T1.

Myc switches on genes involved in cell growth and division, while cyclin T1 helps activate the machinery cells need to multiply. Together, the proteins can encourage mature heart muscle cells to start dividing again.

The researchers used modified mRNA to give heart muscle cells instructions for making the two proteins. This is the same basic technology used in COVID vaccines, which deliver temporary genetic instructions to cells to make a protein that trains the immune system to recognise the virus.

Importantly, mRNA does not need to alter a cell’s DNA. Instead, it provides temporary instructions that are naturally broken down. This temporary activity is particularly important when stimulating cell growth because uncontrolled cell growth is the basis of cancer.
What happened in the damaged hearts?
The researchers tested their approach in mice following experimentally induced heart attacks.

The researchers injected the modified mRNA directly into the damaged hearts of mice that had suffered heart attacks. The treatment activated genes involved in cell division, prompting heart muscle cells to start multiplying. Crucially, the treated mice also showed improvements in heart function.
After 28 days, the treated mice had lost less pumping ability than untreated mice. They also had more heart muscle tissue.
In a longer experiment, improvements in heart function were still evident 12 weeks after treatment.

These findings suggest that temporarily activating the heart’s growth machinery may help restore some of the function lost following injury. However, the treatment did not consistently reduce scar tissue. This suggests that the heart’s improved pumping ability did not necessarily mean damaged muscle had been fully replaced.
One of the most important findings concerns safety. Myc is a powerful regulator of cell growth and is also associated with cancer when its activity becomes uncontrolled.
Activating Myc and cyclin T1 widely throughout the damaged heart could be dangerous. In one experiment, several mice developed severe illness or died.

Restricting activation to a smaller region of heart muscle surrounding the initial injury produced a much more favourable response. The findings highlight a major challenge: researchers must find a way to stimulate heart muscle cells to divide without triggering uncontrolled growth elsewhere in the heart.
Encouragingly, no tumours were observed during the reported follow-up of mice receiving the localised treatment. However, longer studies will be essential to establish safety.

There are substantial obstacles before this approach could be tested routinely in patients. The treatment has not yet been shown to regenerate damaged human hearts. Researchers must work out how to deliver the treatment safely, find the right dose and check for complications such as abnormal heart rhythms and uncontrolled cell growth. Still, the findings are an important advance in regenerative cardiovascular medicine.

For decades, the emphasis after a heart attack has been on preventing further damage and helping the surviving heart muscle work more efficiently. This research points towards a different ambition: replacing some of the muscle that has already been lost.

If future studies demonstrate that the approach is both safe and effective in humans, treating a heart attack might one day involve not only restoring blood flow, but also giving the heart the instructions it needs to repair itself.

articles.title: Spermmaxxing: the science behind ice packs, red light and abstinence
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Some men are taking ice packs into saunas to protect their testicles from the heat. Others are shining red lights on their groins or eating raw butter in the hope of improving their sperm. There are even organised sperm races, with competitors and spectators.

Welcome to spermmaxxing, the latest online trend promising men ways to boost their sperm count and quality. It brings male fertility into the world of internet self-optimisation, where almost any part of the body can become a project.
But do these techniques actually work? And what can sperm count tell someone about their chances of becoming a parent?
In this episode of the Strange Health podcast, I investigate the claims with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Michael Carroll, a reproductive scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University and former NHS clinical embryologist. He helps us explore what the evidence says about sperm health, and where online advice gets ahead of the science.
Why an ice pack is not a fertility plan

Some spermmaxxing ideas begin with a grain of biological truth. Testicles generally need to be cooler than the rest of the body for sperm production to function normally, and repeated exposure to high temperatures may affect sperm quality. But that doesn’t establish that strapping an ice pack to your groin while sitting in a sauna will improve fertility.

Red-light treatments are also being promoted online. Researchers have investigated how particular kinds of light affect sperm in laboratory conditions. Evidence that devices used at home improve men’s chances of fathering a child, however, is lacking. As for a diet built around raw butter and animal products, an impressive-looking plate is no substitute for clinical evidence.

The interest in spermmaxxing is partly fuelled by reports of declining sperm counts. A major review found that average sperm counts fell in the populations it studied over several decades. But a sperm count on its own cannot tell you whether you can conceive. Doctors may also look at how well sperm move and their shape, alongside other aspects of reproductive health.
What happens when fertility becomes a competition?

Dan and I also take a detour into the history of sperm science, beginning with Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who observed moving sperm through a microscope in 1677. Almost 350 years later, sperm racing has turned microscopic movement into an actual spectator event.

There’s a serious subject beneath the spectacle. Male infertility can be distressing, and some causes need medical assessment rather than lifestyle experiments. We explore conditions such as varicocele, enlarged veins around the testicles, and azoospermia, when semen contains no sperm, as well as the treatments that may help.
Listen to the episode to discover what spermmaxxing gets right, where its claims fall short and what men concerned about their fertility can do instead.

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
articles.author: Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago
paras: The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000. A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17.
Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025, as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world. What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95%. But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine.

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963. The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective. A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children. After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99%, and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated.

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.
So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine, measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases.

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia, leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.
In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it.
A surge of outbreaks – and deaths

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized.

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak, which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status.
Fertile ground for misinformation
When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010, and its author lost his medical license. But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day, even though studies that included millions of children have found no link.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience.
Federal policy fuels further confusion
Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots, which are not sold in the United States. There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment, not a cure or vaccine substitute.
Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26. Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2%.

Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.
Adult immunity also has gaps: Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission. That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.
But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.

The Department of Health and Human Services blames current vaccination gaps on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that the agency would not make any changes in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status.
Additionally, orders like August’s about the MMR vaccine, and revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations, are weakening vaccination efforts.

Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible has been substantially weakened.
So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.

articles.title: Why does your body store fat in your butt?
articles.author: Cara Ocobock, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, University of Notre Dame
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why does your body store fat in your butt? - Ellen, age 8, Cambridge, Massachusetts
Have you ever wondered why some parts of your body are firm, like your elbows, while other areas, like your butt, are squishier?
The difference is due to what scientists call fat distribution, and researchers are still trying to understand why bodies store fat in some places but not in others.
All animals have fat in their bodies, even insects. Bears even put on up to 400 pounds (180 kilograms) of additional body fat, the equivalent of 544 large cheese pizzas, to survive hibernation.
Fat is an important and constantly changing part of all bodies, including those of humans and our evolutionary ancestors.
Fat, also called adipose tissue, is one kind of connective tissue that helps hold your body together.

For a long time, scientists thought that adipose tissue was mainly a storage place for the extra energy your body doesn’t use from the food you eat. While fat is a great source of stored energy, it also has many other functions. There are even different kinds of fat.

Visceral fat serves as a sort of protective bubble wrap, surrounding and filling in the spaces between your internal organs. Subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat between your skin and your muscle that you can pinch, is a protective cushion and helps to keep you warm by insulating you like a coat.
Fat also produces and responds to hormones, a type of chemical messenger, to regulate how your body uses energy and to tell you when you are hungry or full.
Different kinds of fat also have different jobs. White fat is the kind of fat most people are familiar with and performs the functions mentioned above.
You may be less familiar with brown fat, which is brown because it contains a lot of mitochondria: the parts of your cells that produce the energy your body needs to perform all its functions.

Not all animals have brown fat, but humans do. Scientists know that brown fat performs a special function to heat your body when you get cold. It doesn’t store energy, like white fat does, to help your body move.

When you were a baby, you had a lot of brown fat along your torso to help keep you warm because your body wasn’t mature enough to maintain your body temperature. As you grow older, you have less brown fat. It is only located just above your collar bone and along your major deep blood vessels, like your aorta.
Why do humans store fat where we do?

Researchers don’t know enough yet about brown fat to know why it is in just a few parts of the body. It is possible that it’s near the neck and around major blood vessels to help insulate the blood and keep overall body temperature in a healthy warm range.
As for white fat, there appear to be three main factors that determine where your fat gets stored: genetics, hormones and age.
Certain genes direct fat to accumulate in the butt, while other genes tell it to collect on the torso.

Hormones like estrogen, which affects almost every system in all bodies but is typically higher in females, direct more subcutaneous fat to gather in the butt, thighs and backs of the arms. Cortisol, the stress hormone, seems to direct visceral fat to accumulate in the belly area.

But why isn’t fat evenly distributed throughout the body? Well, having a lot of fat around your elbows and knees would limit your ability to bend your arms and legs. Storing a lot of fat around your head would possibly put your brain at risk of overheating. Other parts of your body, like hips, butts, breasts and thighs, don’t have these risks – maybe that’s why we store fat there.
Why do people have fat at all?

Don’t be fooled: A lot of animals that look fat, like a hippopotamus, actually aren’t. Hippos only have around 2% body fat, the percentage of how much of your body mass comes from fat; while the average human woman has over 30% body fat.

In the rest of the animal kingdom, biologists typically only see a lot of body fat among hibernating or marine mammals. For the hibernators, the fat serves as energy storage for long, cold winters. For marine mammals like seals and whales, that extra fat is like a giant puffy coat helping to keep them warm in the cold depths of the ocean.
Humans do not hibernate, nor do we live in the ocean, so why do we have a lot more fat than all other primates and most mammals?

Anthropologists like me, who study how the human body has evolved over time, think it has to do with the lifestyle of our evolutionary ancestors who had to gather and hunt to survive. Gathering and hunting were not always reliable food sources. We think our ancestors developed the ability to put on extra fat as a food insurance policy. When food was difficult to find, they could rely on their extra fat stores to carry them through until food became available again.
Researchers are still trying to determine when this extra fat storage evolved. We have one line of evidence from small stone figures known as Gravettian statues.
These ancient statues from 25,000 to 28,000 years ago depict feminine figures who carry a lot of extra body fat. Archaeologists have found them all throughout Europe and Russia.

The way the ancient artists depicted fat on these figures matches how fat looks on bodies today. This accuracy has led researchers to believe that the makers of the Gravettian statues knew how individuals with greater body fat actually looked, meaning at least some people at this time did put on a lot of extra fat.

Europe and Russia back then were much colder than they are today, supporting the idea that our ancestors would have needed the extra fat to get through the extremely cold winters when food was harder to find.
So, the next time you poke at your butt fat, remember that fat is a really important part of our bodies, performs lots of different functions, and is likely evolutionarily ancient for us humans.

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.
